The First Latvian Song Festival: In Riga the choirs have gathered: a thousand singers from the parishes, in white shirts and woven sashes, and the songs have no lords' names in them. The German papers sneer at peasant merriment
French: the Russian governor notes the crowds and files a report. Both miss the point - a nation has heard itself.

The First Latvian Song Festival: Let the whole nation sing!
Song is cheap
The Young Latvians

A circle of schoolmasters and students - the Young Latvians - has opened a newspaper in the farmers' own tongue, arguing that the land's language, land and learning belong to those who plough it, not only to those who own it. The Baltic German press calls them peasants playing at politics.
The press belongs to the people who read it.
The censors should read it first.
Barons and the Dainas

Krisjanis Barons has gathered the dainas - the short songs of the farmers, tens of thousands of them, each four lines old as the plough - into one great cabinet of drawers, one song to a slip. The nation's whole memory in a piece of furniture
French: now the scholars read what the villages never forgot.

The First Latvian Song Festival: Every drawer holds a nation's heart.
The Riga Polytechnic

Riga's merchants and engineers have founded a Polytechnic: chemistry, mechanics, commerce, taught to the sons - and soon the daughters - of the city. German is the lecture language still, but the workshops answer to no man's flag, and the graduates will build the port's cranes, mills and bridges.
A school for the city that builds.
The guilds taught well enough before.
The New Current

A younger generation has outgrown the patriots of the awakening: they call themselves the New Current, they read Marx on smuggled paper, and they ask not for song festivals but for land, wages and the vote. The young socialist workers of Riga's mills do not sing - they organize.
The current cannot be dammed.
The mills will be quiet again.
The Harbor of Riga
Grain, timber, flax and hemp: the Daugava road floats the harvest of a hundred parishes down to Riga's quays, and from Riga's quays to the world. The harbor cranes work from first light to last
French: the stevedores sing in two languages

The First Latvian Song Festival: The harbor feeds the city.
The Latvian Riflemen

The war has come to the Daugava, and the army has called for volunteers: battalions of riflemen, raised from the farms and factories, trained and officered in a manner the old empire never allowed. They ask one question the recruiters do not answer - when the war ends, whose army will they be?
Give them rifles - and remember they are ours.
Lacplesis

Pumpurs' epic is printed: the Bear-Slayer, born of a man and a she-bear, who wrestles the Black Knight for the fate of the land. Every reader knows who the Black Knight is meant to be. The censor apparently did not.
The Bear-Slayer fights again.
The Folk Costumes

On Sundays the old patterns come out of the chests: the great pinned shawls, the silver brooches, the striped skirts of a hundred villages, each stripe a parish's own. The city photographers make postcards of them
French: the young women make something else - a flag without a flagpole.

The First Latvian Song Festival: Wear the grandmother's silver with pride.
The Dairy Cooperatives
The farmers of one parish have built a creamery together: everyone's milk in everyone's churn, and the butter sold under one brand to England. The manor lords called it communism
French: the cooperative's ledger called it a dividend. By autumn every district wants one.

The First Latvian Song Festival: One churn, one purse, one butter.
Let each churn his own.
The Year 1905

The news from Petersburg has lit the Baltic countryside: farmhands strike, teachers resign, crowds burn the manor record-books in the yard - the old serf registers, the debt rolls, the lists of dues. The punitive columns answer with the birch rod and the gallows. An old order is ending badly.
Let the old ledgers burn!
Send the columns - restore quiet.
The Press Ban

By imperial decree, not a single letter shall be printed in Lithuanian with our letters: the language may exist, but only in the Russian alphabet. The printing shops cross the border into East Prussia
French: the books come back across it in coal sacks, under sled loads, inside bibles.

The First Latvian Song Festival: The knygnesys ride by night.
The border guards earn their pay tonight.
Ausra

From a press in far-off Ragnit the first number of Ausra - the Dawn - has crossed the border in the coal sacks: a Lithuanian newspaper, in Lithuanian letters, for a people forbidden both. The dawn metaphor is not subtle. It is not meant to be.
The dawn comes over the border by night.
A newspaper is a small thing.
Basanavicius Calls the Revival

From his study abroad the scholar has called on every Lithuanian who can hold a pen to write down the songs, the tales, the customs of the farms - a nation, he says, that does not know itself cannot be itself. Committees form
German: the farms learn that their grandmothers' songs are history.

The First Latvian Song Festival: Write down everything the grandmothers remember.
The Great Vilnius Seimas

Two thousand delegates have crowded into Vilnius - farmers, priests, workers - and voted: Lithuania declares herself a nation, with a language, a land, and a say in her own affairs. The empire calls it an assembly of malcontents. The delegates call it the first session.
Lithuania has spoken: she exists!
Two thousand malcontents, one gendarme each.
The Land Bank
The manors sell
French: the farmers buy - but not with cash, with credit: a land bank to lend the purchase price against the harvest, so that the ploughmen may own what they plough. Within a decade the estate ledger-books pass from lords' desks to farmers' strongboxes.

The First Latvian Song Festival: Lend the farmers their own land.
Credit is for merchants, not muzhiks.
The Question of the Letters

The printers quarrel over the hard facts of the alphabet: the Polish l, the Slavic sz, the tails and hooks borrowed from the manor houses' Polish bibles. The farmers in the end keep the letters their grandmothers sang in - and the smuggled books all use them.
Keep the letters of the grandmothers.
The Cholera Year

The sickness has come up the roads from the ports: villages emptied, quarantines broken by frightened neighbors, the parish priests reading the last rites through cloth masks. The doctors ask for a sanitary cordon and the money to keep it
French: the governor asks who will pay.

The First Latvian Song Festival: Whatever it costs - hold the cordon.
The plague always passes.
The Science Society

Basanavicius has come home, and with him the Lithuanian Science Society: archaeology in the burial mounds, dictionaries, folklore in matching notebooks, a museum with a buying budget. The farms send in their old pagan stones when the plough turns them up.
Dig, collect, remember, publish.
An Anthem for the Nation

Kudirka's hymn is sung first by schoolchildren, then by everyone: 'Thy hills, thy lowlands, our native land' - a song for a country that does not yet sit on any map. The gendarmes copy out the lyrics into their files
French: the children teach them to their parents.

The First Latvian Song Festival: Our native land, our dearest one.
The Boats from Memel

From the little port the emigrants board for Hamburg and thence the Atlantic: whole villages of miners' sons bound for the coal of Pennsylvania, farm girls for the mills of New England. The shipping agents' handbills promise everything
French: the letters home, less - but they enclose money orders.

The First Latvian Song Festival: Let them go - and send the money home.
The villages are emptying!
